segments.text: The Revolution destroyed the political structure of the ancien régime and spread new ideas of citizenship, legal equality and nationalism across Europe; Napoleon both preserved and restricted parts of that inheritance, and the correct exam approach is to evaluate which revolutionary changes he institutionalised and which political freedoms he restricted, rather than asking whether he was simply “for” or “against” the Revolution.

French society was legally divided into privileged estates, while the monarchy faced heavy debt and an unequal tax system that repeated fiscal-reform attempts failed to solve, since privileged groups resisted and the monarchy lacked a workable political mechanism to impose change. In 1789, the Estates-General transformed into the National Assembly, the Bastille fell, feudal privileges were attacked, and the
Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

articulated new principles of legal equality, national sovereignty and individual rights. An initial attempt to retain a constitutional monarchy collapsed under the pressure of war, royal distrust, and political radicalisation, and the monarchy was abolished in

, reorganised education, and reached a settlement with the Catholic Church — changes that strengthened the state while preserving significant parts of the Revolution’s legal transformation, even as he curtailed political liberty and crowned himself Emperor in 1804. Military expansion spread French influence but generated resistance everywhere it reached; the Continental System, the Peninsular War (covered from Britain’s side in British History Topic 6), the disastrous Russian campaign, and repeated coalitions exhausted the empire, ending in defeat in 1814 and finally at Waterloo in 1815.

items.text: Napoleon’s codification of civil law, preserving revolutionary legal equality while consolidating centralised state authority.
The unstable moderate-republican government (1795–99) whose weaknesses opened the way for Napoleon’s coup.

Prepare the Revolution in stages: causes → moderate phase → radical republic/Terror → Directory → Napoleon; make a separate Napoleon sheet for domestic reforms, military expansion and causes of defeat.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “Which revolutionary changes did Napoleon institutionalise, and which did he restrict?”
Do not explain the Revolution only through Enlightenment ideas; financial, social and political crises were equally important.
Do not treat the Revolution as one continuous radical phase; its aims and institutions changed repeatedly.
Do not call Napoleon either purely a “child” or purely a “betrayer” of the Revolution; evaluate what he preserved and what he restricted.
France’s fiscal crisis and political deadlock helped trigger the Estates-General in 1789.
The monarchy was abolished and France became a republic in 1792.
The Reign of Terror reached its height in 1793–94.
Napoleon became First Consul after the 1799 coup and Emperor in 1804.
The Napoleonic Code and administrative centralisation had lasting influence; military overstretch and renewed coalitions contributed to his downfall by 1815.

Evaluate Napoleon by what he institutionalised (legal equality, administrative centralisation) versus what he restricted (political liberty), never by a simple “for or against the Revolution” verdict.
The Revolution’s multiple, distinct phases (constitutional monarchy, radical republic, Directory) must be kept analytically separate, since their aims and institutions genuinely differed.
